fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, "Let your hands be strong, you who now hear these words spoken by the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid to rebuild the temple…" He's talking to people who have work in front of them. And strong hands are exactly what any work needs, even stamping cookies.

True, friend. The ones doing the inviting say, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." Then they add, "I myself am going." That's not a "you go ahead, I'll catch up later." They're in.
That's it, baker. God says, "I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem." The One returning is the LORD Himself. Then Jerusalem gets a brand new name, which is coming up.

That one points the other way, friend. God says the opposite about His people. "I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem…" He says (Zechariah 8:8). So this is a gathering promise, not a scattering one.

You got it, baker. God says, "…the mountain of the LORD of Hosts will be called the Holy Mountain." Jerusalem gets the name City of Truth, and the mountain gets its own name too. A city and a mountain, each with a new name.

The Mount of Olives is a real hill, baker, and the apostles returned to Jerusalem from it (Acts 1:12). It's just not the name God gives here. He says, "…the mountain of the LORD of Hosts will be called the Holy Mountain." Sometimes the answer is sitting right in the verse.

Yes, baker. God says, "Old men and old women will again sit along the streets of Jerusalem, each with a staff in hand because of great age." Notice the word "again." Sitting along the streets is the whole picture here.

Not quite, friend. God doesn't say the remnant sees better. He sets two sets of eyes side by side: what looks impossible to them, and what He sees. Then He asks, "…should it also be impossible in My eyes?" His point is that what seems impossible to them is not impossible for Him.

Priests aren't mentioned in this verse, baker. God speaks to people who now hear words spoken by the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid. His message to them is, "Let your hands be strong…" He doesn't hand the job off to anyone else.

Yes, baker. God says, "As you have been a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you will be a blessing." Same people, but a flip from curse to blessing. Then He adds, "Do not be afraid; let your hands be strong."

The verse goes a different direction, friend. God says He has resolved "…to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah." The disaster He mentions is what He resolved back then, when the fathers provoked Him to anger (Zechariah 8:14). Disaster on all the nations isn't what this verse says.

You got it, baker. God says the fasts of the fourth, the fifth, the seventh and the tenth months "…will become times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts for the house of Judah." Those four fasts get a whole new meaning. And this is how the passage answers the fasting question from the beginning (Zechariah 7:3).

Yes, baker. The residents of one city will go to another, saying, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." They don't say it to themselves. They say it to the people in the other city.
